exercise_group.instruction: Exercises 9–16 relate to a primal linear programming problem of finding $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ so as to maximize $$f(\textbf{x}) = \textbf{c}^{T}\textbf{x}$$ subject to $$A\textbf{x} \leq \textbf{b}$$ and $$\textbf{x} \geq 0$$ . Mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer.

problem.paragraph: (T/F) The dual problem is to minimize $$\textbf{y}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ subject to $$A\textbf{y} \geq \textbf{c}$$ and $$\textbf{y} \geq \textbf{0}$$ .
(T/F) The dual of the dual problem is the original primal problem.
(T/F) If both the primal and the dual problems are feasible, then they both have optimal solutions.
(T/F) If either the primal or the dual problem has an optimal solution, then they both do.

(T/F) If $$\overset{‾}{\textbf{x}}$$ is an optimal solution to the primal problem and $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is a feasible solution to the dual problem such that $$g(\widehat{\textbf{y}}) = f(\overset{‾}{\textbf{x}})$$ , then $$g(\widehat{\textbf{y}})$$ is an optimal solution to the dual problem.
(T/F) If the primal problem has an optimal solution, then the final tableau in the simplex method also gives the optimal solution to the dual problem.
(T/F) If a slack variable is in an optimal solution, then the marginal value of the item corresponding to its equation is positive.
(T/F) When a linear programming problem and its dual are used to solve a matrix game, the vectors $$\textbf{u}$$ and $$\textbf{v}$$ are unit.

exercise_group.instruction: Sometimes a minimization problem has inequalities only of the “ $$\geq$$ ” type. In this case, replace the problem by its dual. (Multiplying the original inequalities by $$- 1$$ to reverse their direction will not work, because the basic solution of the initial simplex tableau in this case will be infeasible.) In Exercises 17–20, use the simplex method to solve the dual, and from this solve the original problem (the dual of the dual).

Bob wishes to invest $$\$ \text{35,000}$$ in stocks, bonds, and gold coins. He knows that his rate of return will depend on the economic climate of the country, which is, of course, difficult to predict. After careful analysis, he determines the annual profit in dollars he would expect per hundred dollars on each type of investment, depending on whether the economy is strong, stable, or weak:
Let $$P$$ be a (primal) linear programming problem with feasible set $$\mathcal{F}$$ , and let $$P^{\ast}$$ be the dual problem with feasible set $$\mathcal{F}^{\ast}$$ . Prove the following:

list.item: If $$\mathbf{x}$$ is in $$\mathcal{F}$$ and $$\mathbf{y}$$ is in $$\mathcal{F}^{\ast}$$ , then $$f(\textbf{x}) \leq g(\textbf{y})$$ . [Hint: Write $$f(\textbf{x})$$ as $$\textbf{x}^{T}\textbf{c}$$ and $$g(\textbf{y})$$ as $$\textbf{y}^{T}\textbf{ b}$$ . Then begin with the inequality $$\textbf{c} \leq A^{T}\textbf{y}$$ .]

If $$f(\mathbf{\hat{x}}) = g(\mathbf{\hat{y}})$$ for some $$\mathbf{\hat{x}}$$ in $$\mathcal{F}$$ and $$\mathbf{\hat{y}}$$ in $$\mathcal{F}^{\ast}$$ , then $$\mathbf{\hat{x}}$$ is an optimal solution to $$P$$ and $$\mathbf{\hat{y}}$$ is an optimal solution to $$P^{\ast}$$ .

problem.paragraph: Let $$A$$ be an $$m \times n$$ matrix game. Let $$\mathbf{\overline{y}}$$ and $$\mathbf{\overline{x}}$$ be the optimal solutions to the related primal and dual linear programming problems, respectively, as in the discussion prior to Example 5. Let $$\text{λ} = \textbf{u}^{T}\mathbf{\overline{x}} = \textbf{v}^{T}\mathbf{\overline{y}}$$ , and define $$\mathbf{\hat{x}} = \mathbf{\overline{x}}/ \text{λ}$$ and $$\mathbf{\hat{y}} = \mathbf{\overline{y}}/ \text{λ}$$ . Let $$R$$ and $$C$$ , respectively, denote the row and column players.

list.item: Show that $$\mathbf{\hat{x}}$$ and $$\mathbf{\hat{y}}$$ are mixed strategies for $$R$$ and $$C$$ , respectively.
If $$\mathbf{y}$$ is any mixed strategy for $$C$$ , show that $$E(\mathbf{\hat{x}},\mathbf{y}) \geq 1/ \text{λ}$$ .
If $$\mathbf{x}$$ is any mixed strategy for $$R$$ , show that $$E(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{\hat{y}}) \leq 1/ \text{λ}$$ .
Conclude that $$\mathbf{\hat{x}}$$ and $$\mathbf{\hat{y}}$$ are optimal mixed strategies for $$R$$ and $$C$$ , respectively, and that the value of the game is $$1/ \text{λ}$$ .

image.alt: A two-way table lists the potential rate of returns for three types of investments in three economic conditions categorized as strong, stable, and weak.

list.item: How should Bob invest his money in order to maximize his profit regardless of what the economy does? That is, consider the problem as a matrix game in which Bob, the row player, is playing against the “economy.” What is the expected value of his portfolio at the end of the year?

problem.paragraph: The slack variables are $$x_{3}$$ , $$x_{4}$$ , and $$x_{5}$$ . The bottom row entries in these columns of the final simplex tableau give the optimal solution to the dual problem. Thus $$\bar{\mathbf{y}} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} .$$

Slack variable $$x_{3}$$ comes from the constraint inequality for fescue. This corresponds to variable $$y_{1}$$ in the dual problem, so the marginal value of fescue is $$0$$ . Similarly, $$x_{4}$$ and $$x_{5}$$ come from rye and bluegrass, respectively, so their marginal values are both equal to $$1$$ .
